fields.Front: What annotation marks a method as a JUnit 5 test?
What does @BeforeEach do in a JUnit 5 test class?
fields.Back: Runs the annotated method before every test method in the class — used for per-test setup (e.g. re-creating fixtures).

fields.Front: What does @AfterEach do in a JUnit 5 test class?
fields.Back: Runs the annotated method after every test method — used for per-test cleanup (e.g. closing resources).

fields.Front: Write a JUnit 5 test asserting that 2 + 2 equals 4.
Write a JUnit 5 test asserting that calc.divide(1, 0) throws ArithmeticException.
fields.Back:
@Test
void divideByZeroThrows() {
    Calculator calc = new Calculator();
    assertThrows(ArithmeticException.class,
        () -> calc.divide(1, 0));
}

fields.Front: What does JUnit's assertThrows(...) return, and why is that useful?
fields.Back: It returns the caught exception instance, so you can chain further assertions on it (e.g. assertEquals("bad input", ex.getMessage())) instead of only checking the type.

fields.Front: Write a JUnit 5 parameterized test that checks every int in {1, 2, 3, 4} is positive.
In Mockito, what does the @Mock annotation create?
fields.Back: A fake implementation of the annotated type whose methods return default/empty values (null, 0, empty collection, etc.) until you stub them — it does not call any real logic.
Creates a real instance of the class under test and injects the fields annotated @Mock (or @Spy) into it via constructor, setter, or field injection.

fields.Front: Write Mockito code to stub userRepository.findById(1L) so it returns Optional.of(user).
Why must you use doReturn(x).when(mock).method() instead of when(mock.method()).thenReturn(x) when stubbing a Mockito spy?
fields.Back: when(...) first actually calls mock.method() to resolve the argument; on a spy that wraps a real object, that invokes the real method (possibly with side effects) before the stub is applied. doReturn() never calls the real method.

fields.Front: How do you verify with Mockito that emailService.send(...) was called exactly once?
fields.Back:
verify(emailService, times(1)).send(any());
(times(1) is the default, so verify(emailService).send(any()); is equivalent.)

fields.Front: What is the rule for mixing Mockito argument matchers (like anyString()) with raw literal values in the same stub or verify call?
fields.Back: If any argument in the call uses a matcher, all arguments in that call must be matchers — you cannot mix raw values and matchers in one invocation (use eq(value) for the raw ones instead).

fields.Front: What do the three parts of the AAA pattern stand for when structuring a unit test?
fields.Back: Arrange (set up objects/data), Act (call the method under test), Assert (check the result) — keeping these visually separated makes tests easier to read.

fields.Front: Write a JUnit 5 + Mockito test for a Spring OrderService that mocks its OrderRepository dependency, without starting the Spring context.
fields.Back:
@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class OrderServiceTest {
    @Mock OrderRepository repo;
    @InjectMocks OrderService service;

    @Test
    void savesOrder() {
        when(repo.save(any())).thenReturn(new Order());
        assertNotNull(service.createOrder());
    }
}
A test double that wraps a real object; unless explicitly stubbed, calling a method on it runs the real implementation — unlike a mock, which returns defaults for every unstubbed call.

fields.Text: In JUnit 5, {{c1::@BeforeAll}} runs once before all tests in the class, and {{c2::@AfterAll}} runs once after all tests; both must be static methods unless the class uses @TestInstance(Lifecycle.PER_CLASS).

A JUnit 5 parameterized test uses {{c1::@ParameterizedTest}} instead of @Test, plus a source annotation such as {{c2::@ValueSource}}, {{c3::@CsvSource}}, or {{c4::@MethodSource}} to supply the argument values.
